newsitem.title: QATAR: India in talks to buy Qatari LNG.
newsitem.headline: India in talks to buy Qatari LNG.

text.p: India is discussing buying up to five million tonnes a year of Qatari liquefied natural gas (LNG), a senior Indian official said on Wednesday.
But an agreement could be signed after India succeeds in clinching a deal on the "lowest price", said Vijay Kelkar, secretary to the Indian ministry of petroleum and natural gas.

"We have floated a global tender, and Qatar's Ras Laffan LNG Company is among 17 international LNG players which have submitted offers to supply gas", he said after a two-day visit to Qatar, home to the world's largest gas reserve after Russia and Iran.
"But the lowest price, besides the security of supply, is our main concern".
Kelkar, accompanied by the chairman of the Gas Authority of India Ltd, met Qatar's Minister of Energy and Industry, Abdullah bin Hamad al-Attiyah, and other energy officials.
They also toured Ras Laffan -- the site of the Gulf Arab state's three major LNG projects north of the capital Doha.
Kelkar said India had been trying to import gas via pipeline from Oman and Iran. But both projects could not get off the ground for feasibilty reasons.
"More data about reserves are awaited on the Oman-India pipleine," he said.

"And a feasibility study on the Iran-India pipeline by a German company, appointed for the job, could not start because of the lack of an approval from Pakistan which has economic zone control over part of the route", he explained.
"Qatar could be the major and most promising source of LNG supply --the third option -- to India because of its vast gas reserves and proximity to India", said Kelkar.
"They (Qataris) are also very keen to supply India and the minister has in principle welcomed India's participation in one of the Qatari projects", he said.
He was referring to an Indian request in December to take a stake in Ras Laffan LNG Company (RASGAS). No decision has been taken yet.

The Qatar General Petroleum Corporation owns 66.5 percent of RASGAS shares while U.S. oil giant Mobil Corp has a 26.5 percent stake. Japan's Nisshow Iwai has four percent and Ittochu has three percent.
Kelkar said India's energy needs were growing at eight to 10 percent a year.
"Presently we need a minimum of 122 million cubic metres of gas a day, but our supply, mainly through domestic production, is just half of that".
"Initially we need five million tonnes of LNG annually. But this will increase dramatically by 2001", he said.
